To investigate this, we analyzed multidimensioinal simulations within Magnetohydrodinamics incorporating both diffusive decay and beam streaming under a pressure-dominated cosmic rays regime . The simulations showed an EDDINGION LIMIT below gravity where rays are effectively ejected by CRs into astrophysics driven outflows. Our analysis concluded that high energy photons contribute substantially to driving galactic winds over wide ranges despite uncertainties regarding transport models of cosmic rays into plasma environments including supereddin regime fluxes where energy transfers dominate momentum dynamics between radiation, gas particles or thermal dissipation in plasma environments . The simulations revealed significant asymmetries between radiation forces and plasma magnetic tension forces as well as saturation effects when cosmic rays reach critical intensities . Most importantly , our model predicts that even when cosmic rays reach critical intensities due radiative cooling , most momentum is carried away through radiative loss although residual heat deposition continues driving significant structural outflows. This work implies cosmic rays effectively mobilise atmospheric energy reservoirs regardless of complex feedback processes influencing momentum transport efficiency. Notable is how streaming-induced instabilities affect thermal dissipation versus bulk motions in outflow structures influenced simultaneously by CRs, magneto- thermal equilibrium, cooling radiation, and plasma turbulence . Overall we showed cosmic rays are integral components for generating the observed feedback processes within active regions . Radiative loss mechanisms remain secondary unless they exceed critical flux thresholds at which point mass erosion dominates dynamical response due gravitational confinement being insufficient .
